title: Redwood structured output & function-calling demo - Stratus Insights
summary: Intro/demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode) and function/tool calling. Walkthrough of console JSON schema editor, guardrails, and runtime behavior. Discussed onboarding pilot, security docs, and next steps to run a 48-hour pilot and share sample payloads for benchmarking.
next_steps: Ben to send SOC2 + security pack and pricing by 2026-06-18
Samir to share sample JSON schemas and guardrail config by 2026-06-18
Stratus to share representative payloads and success metrics by 2026-06-19
Schedule POC scoping call with infra (aim: within 1 week)
action_items: Ben Armitage: Send pricing + pilot onboarding guide: 2026-06-18
Samir Patel: Share sample JSON schema examples and guardrail templates: 2026-06-18
Alex Morgan: Provide sample input payloads and latency targets: 2026-06-19
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-17 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~48m | Attendees: Ben (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Alex (Stratus), Priya (Stratus), Carlos (Stratus)

[00:00] Ben: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm Ben Armitage from Redwood, AE on this account. Samir's the SE and he'll do most of the demo. how's everyone's afternoon?
[00:06] Priya: Good, thanks. we just wrapped a sprint so perfect timing.
[00:09] Carlos: hi, good to meet you both. we're excited — we've been evaluating structured outputs for our insights product.
[00:14] Samir: Awesome. quick agenda — we'll walk through the structured output JSON mode, show function/tool calling in a sample flow, jump into the console to show schema editor and guardrails, and finish with pilot options and next steps. sound good?
[00:24] Alex: yes, that's great. we're especially interested in schema enforcement and how to ensure downstream systems don't break on weird model outputs.
[00:31] Samir: Totally. that's exactly what JSON mode+guardrails helps with. i'll start with a quick slide — this is essentially Redwood's structured output: you can define a JSON schema for the model to follow and the runtime validates and optionally enforces it. there are also recovery policies if the model drifts.
[00:47] Ben: stacking on that, we support two enforcement modes — soft validation where outputs are annotated with issues, and strict mode where the runtime will retry or call a fallback function to repair the output.
[00:59] Priya: retry how? is that deterministic or just another model call that might still fail?
[01:05] Samir: good question. the retry logic is pluggable — you can configure a repair function (we call it a tool) which receives the raw text and the schema errors and returns a corrected JSON blob. that tool can be a simple Redwood-hosted repair assistant or an HTTP webhook to your service.
[01:22] Alex: so it's function-calling under the hood. how many retries are allowed? and does that affect cost?
[01:29] Samir: you can set the retry budget — default is 2 retries. each retry is another model invocation so yes, counted in tokens; however we show token-level cost in Console and Optimize suggests batching/quant profiles to reduce unit cost.
[01:41] Carlos: what about latency impact? our SLA is 300ms tail for quick lookups and the structured outputs might add overhead.
[01:49] Ben: we recommend pinning a lower-latency variant or using dedicated capacity for those hot paths. also caching and prefix KV cache reduce repeat costs/latency for deterministic parts of the prompt.
[01:59] Priya: can you show a live example? like a product-extract flow returning a typed JSON schema?
[02:05] Samir: sure, i'll share my screen — starting with the Playground in Console. (screen share) okay, i have a sample prompt 'extract product info from review' and a simple schema: { name: string, price: number, categories: [string], in_stock: boolean, specs: { weight: string? } } — note, optional fields allowed.
[02:30] Alex: minor nit — if the model returns price as '$12.00' and schema expects number, will it coerce?
[02:36] Samir: by default validation would fail. but in the guardrail you can add a coercion/repair step: either enable 'coerce strings to numbers' heuristics or wire a repair tool that strips symbols and parses floats.
[02:49] Ben: also Console shows the validation errors inline so you can see which fields failed and why.
[02:54] Priya: cool. can you demo function calling as part of the flow? e.g., call our pricing service if price missing?
[03:01] Samir: yep. i'll add a tool binding — here's an HTTP tool called 'price_lookup' pointing to a mock endpoint. then in the flow i set 'on_missing: call price_lookup' for price field.
[03:16] Alex: what's the auth story for webhooks?
[03:19] Samir: we support signed request headers and you can use a Vault/KMS integration for keys. for Private deployments you can even use your internal network.
[03:27] Carlos: any logs/audit for those tool calls? we need traceability.
[03:31] Ben: yes, every tool call is logged in the request trace; Console includes per-request call tree and timestamps. enterprise plans can route logs to your SIEM.
[03:41] Samir: demo time — i'll trigger inference. note that i'm in JSON mode so model is asked to return a JSON object complying with schema.
[03:49] [03:49] Model: {"name":"Stellar Blender", "price":"$129.99", "categories":["kitchen","appliances"], "in_stock":"yes"}
[03:59] Samir: as you can see the model returned price as a string and in_stock as 'yes' string. runtime flagged validation errors: price type mismatch, in_stock not boolean. with soft mode it would annotate — with strict mode it'll try remediation.
[04:14] Ben: i'll switch the route to strict enforcement for this demo and enable the repair tool.
[04:20] Samir: triggering again...
[04:24] [04:24] Model: {"name":"Stellar Blender", "price":"$129.99", "categories":["kitchen","appliances"], "in_stock":"yes"}
[04:33] [04:33] Tool(price_repair webhook): received raw output + errors, returning repaired JSON
[04:39] [04:39] Tool Response: {"name":"Stellar Blender", "price":129.99, "categories":["kitchen","appliances"], "in_stock":true}
[04:46] Samir: repaired successfully. Console shows the call chain: model -> validation -> repair tool -> final output.
[04:54] Priya: nice. one follow-up — does the repair tool run in-line synchronously? any timeout considerations?
[05:00] Samir: yes synchronous by default. you can set tool timeout at route level; default 2s. for high latency tools we support async patterns where the model returns a correlation id and your service later posts the resolved object.
[05:12] Alex: for us async might be fine for background enrichments but for UI we need sub-300ms. i'll need to understand cost of dedicated vs hosted.
[05:20] Ben: we can model that in a small benchmark — we have previous results showing dedicated pinned model variants + reduced quantization variance yields <200ms median on A100-ish clusters for small seq len. we'll share the spreadsheet.
[05:33] Carlos: quantization — are you recommending 4-bit for production? we worry about hallucination/regression.
[05:39] Samir: Redwood Optimize produces recommendations per workload. for highly structured extraction we often use a quantized variant with additional calibration and regression tests; Optimize will suggest a candidate with expected latency and an estimated quality delta. you can also run golden prompt evals to detect regressions.
[05:55] Priya: can we tie evals to our success criteria? e.g., exact-field match for product_id and price tolerance?
[06:01] Samir: absolutely. Console's evals support custom metrics and threshold alerts; if accuracy drops the rollout can automatically rollback to previous model.
[06:09] Ben: let's switch to the Console route config to show the policies — rate limits, retry budgets, fallback model.
[06:15] [06:15] Samir: (shows console) here's route 'product-extract-v1' configured for strict JSON mode, retry_budget=2, fallback_model=smaller-llm, enrichment_tools=[price_lookup], rate_limit=300rpm. you can see tracing hooks and cost per-token estimate.
[06:34] Alex: what's the billing model for tool calls — do they count separately?
[06:38] Ben: tool calls that invoke the model are billed as model tokens; simple webhook repair responses are not billed by us beyond network egress. we show detailed breakdowns so you can see where tokens are spent.
[06:50] Priya: can we demo a failure mode — model returning nested unexpected object — and show how guardrails handle it?
[06:57] Samir: yep. i'll force a bad response.
[07:02] [07:02] Model: {"name": ["Stellar","Blender"], "price": {"amount":"129.99","currency":"usd"}, "unexpected": {"foo":"bar"}}
[07:12] Samir: runtime flagged 'name not string', 'price not number', and an unrecognized 'unexpected' field. with schema_strict + drop_unexpected=true, runtime will attempt to drop unknown keys then call repair tool for type coercion.
[07:25] Ben: note you can also enable 'reject_on_unexpected' to surface errors back to the caller instead of repairing silently — helpful for audit-critical flows.
[07:34] Carlos: that sounds good. in terms of compliance, can we get audit logs with the original raw output and the final repaired output? we need to show lineage for SOC2.
[07:42] Ben: yes, audit trail includes raw model output, validation errors, tool call responses, and final output. retention and log shipping configurable per plan.
[07:51] Samir: jumping now to function-calling patterns — besides simple repair tools, you can bind tools as domain ops: price_lookup, inventory_fetch, product_normalize. tools can be HTTP, internal RPC, or Redwood-hosted lambdas.
[08:05] Alex: can we run our existing internal microservice as a tool (it's on isolated VPC)?
[08:09] Samir: for Private deployments you can route to internal endpoints via VPC peering. for Dedicated you can set up secure egress rules. keys can be stored in KMS, HSM.
[08:18] Priya: how do you handle secrets in tool configs?
[08:21] Samir: we integrate with customer KMS and also support Vault. secrets are never surfaced in Console logs; we show masked traces and offer per-route redaction.
[08:32] Carlos: good. one more: are tool call failures considered retriable for the model flow?
[08:37] Samir: yes, each tool has retry policy; you can set fallback behavior — continue with null, call fallback tool, or abort and return error to caller.
[08:46] Ben: let's talk about observability — Console has per-request token-level cost, latency breakdown (model vs tool), and error codes. here's a saved trace from a previous demo showing tool calls spikes.
[08:58] Priya: can we hook traces to our Datadog?
[09:01] Ben: yep, log shipping to any SIEM or tracing system via webhooks or S3.
[09:06] Alex: curious about developer ergonomics — do you have SDK support for function bindings?
[09:11] Samir: SDKs in Python/Node have helper decorators to register tools and schema definitions; you can also push schema JSON to the Console API.
[09:20] Priya: for our internal teams, we want to enforce a central schema registry — is there an API?
[09:24] Samir: Console exposes a schema catalog API; you can reference schema ids in routes. RBAC supports restricting who can edit schemas.
[09:33] Carlos: can we demo the schema editor?
[09:36] Samir: sure — (screen) here's the visual editor and the raw JSON view. i can add examples, constraints, required fields, and custom validators. watch me add a pattern constraint for SKU format.
[09:50] Alex: that pattern will run client-side or server-side?
[09:53] Samir: server-side during validation. you can also include regex checks and custom JS validators run in a sand-boxed function.
[10:02] Priya: sandboxed JS — is that safe? what's the exec timeout?
[10:06] Samir: sandboxed with strict CPU/memory limits, default 50ms CPU, configurable up to a point. designed for light-weight validation only. heavy work should be offloaded to tools.
[10:18] Ben: circling back to costs and pilot — we often propose a short 48-hour pilot: we deploy a small dedicated pool or use hosted with burst, run ~10k requests across your sample data, and produce a latency/cost/accuracy matrix. recommended next step?
[10:33] Alex: yes please. i'll need the exact data format we'll send and credentials setup for any webhooks.
[10:38] Ben: Samir will share the schema templates and a sample spreadsheet with the request shape. we'll also include security docs and an onboarding checklist.
[10:46] Priya: timeline — we want to start pilot next week if possible.
[10:49] Ben: sounds doable, pending legal/compliance sign-off. we'll aim to start onboarding next Tue if Stratus can share payloads by Friday.
[10:57] Carlos: procurement question — do you allow short-term commitment for dedicated capacity or is it strictly monthly?
[11:02] Ben: Dedicated usually needs a minimum monthly reservation, but for pilots we can support a short-term eval on hosted with dedicated-features enabled, or partner with our Solutions team for a trial agreement.
[11:16] Samir: ok demo — one more advanced pattern: multi-tool orchestration. i'll show an example where model calls price_lookup and inventory_fetch in parallel, and the route aggregates results into final schema.
[11:26] [11:26] Samir: (trigger) Model called price_lookup, inventory_fetch. price_lookup returned price and currency. inventory_fetch returned stock and warehouse_id. runtime merged results using merge rules defined in schema.
[11:39] Priya: merging rules — can we prioritize certain tool results over model output?
[11:43] Samir: yes you can set precedence: tool>model or model>tool per field. good for cases where your canonical data source should override heuristics.
[11:51] Alex: security again — will tool responses be stored in Redwood logs? we need to know retention policies.
[11:56] Ben: default retention 90d, configurable. sensitive fields can be redacted. enterprise plans allow longer retention and on-prem log storage.
[12:06] Priya: what's the troubleshooting workflow if a field continuously fails validation in production?
[12:11] Samir: Console will surface a failing prompt set and you can create an eval suite; Optimize will suggest model/quant config changes and we can pin to a previous model or route traffic gradually with rollouts.
[12:23] Ben: also we have regression alerts tied to golden prompts — you get a slack/email when accuracy dips.
[12:30] Carlos: any mention of competitor differences? we briefly looked at OpenAI function calling and Vertex. how are you different?
[12:36] Ben: our differentiation is production-grade serving — unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, more ops controls like repair tool patterns, richer console for schema lifecycle, and Optimize to recommend configs by workload.
[12:51] Priya: ok can we talk about SSO, RBAC and who on our side will have admin rights?
[12:57] Ben: we support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and RBAC roles. typically product/infra get admin and devs get read/write to routes. we'll share a recommended role mapping for Stratus.
[13:09] Alex: how about model provenance and versioning? we need to pin model versions per route for audits.
[13:15] Samir: yes route pins model version; Console keeps history of model rollouts and you can freeze a version.
[13:21] Priya: anything else in the demo?
[13:24] Samir: quick note on edge cases: for numeric comparisons we support tolerance configs and numeric normalization steps so small formatting differences don't fail strict checks.
[13:35] Carlos: ok, this is helpful. i do want to see a live sample of the pilot config and the expected deliverables. can you walk through a sample pilot plan?
[13:43] Ben: sure — (share doc) Pilot plan: scope data, configure route, baseline test, run 10k requests over 48h, produce report with cost/latency/accuracy, run 2 model variants, suggest Optimize settings. deliverables: report, dashboard access, and recommended route configs.
[14:05] Alex: sounds good. for the 10k requests we'll throw a representative mix: 70% short lookup, 20% long descriptions, 10% noisy OCR text.
[14:14] Samir: perfect that'll stress validation and repair paths.
[14:18] Priya: legal — can you share the standard DPA and security questionnaire?
[14:23] Ben: yes, will attach. we'll also include SOC2 and ISO info where available.
[14:28] Carlos: are there any known model regressions when running strict JSON mode with aggressive quantization?
[14:34] Samir: some quantized variants can have slight semantic shifts; that's why we recommend regression tests and Optimize's calibration. many customers run a small AB test before full rollout.
[14:45] Priya: ok, last question: how do we handle schema evolution — e.g., adding new optional fields mid-prod?
[14:51] Samir: Console supports versioned schemas and you can have route mapping rules to accept multiple schema versions or run a migration pipeline. we also support deprecation warnings and staged rollouts.
[15:05] Ben: great, let's summarize action items and next steps.
[15:09] Ben: (recap) Ben to send security docs and pricing; Samir to share schema templates and guardrail examples; Stratus to provide sample payloads and success criteria; schedule pilot kickoff.
[15:21] Priya: thank you both, this was very thorough.
[15:24] Carlos: thanks. we'll sync internally and aim to get payloads by Friday.
[15:28] Alex: one minor nit — can you also share the console permalink for the demo route so our infra folks can look?
[15:33] Samir: will share permalink in follow-up email along with recording.
[15:38] Ben: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll follow up with a calendar invite for pilot scoping.
[15:43] Priya: thanks, bye.
[15:45] Carlos: bye.

Notes/auto-summary: The team demonstrated Redwood's JSON structured-output mode, schema validation and enforcement modes (soft vs strict), repair tools (synchronous webhooks), and function/tool calling patterns (price_lookup, inventory_fetch). Console features shown: schema editor, route policies (retry budgets, fallback models), observability (per-request traces and token cost), and Optimize recommendations for quantization and batching. Security/compliance discussed: SOC2, KMS/Vault, SSO/SCIM, audit logs. Pilot plan agreed: 48-hour run, ~10k requests, deliverable report.

References shared: demo recording link (TBD), sample schema templates (link), pilot spreadsheet benchmark (link).
